=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Key buyer push-backs

### 1. Bluefen consent must be a Completion condition, not an endeavours obligation
**Issue:** Bluefen represents about **$3.6m / 30% of FY26 revenue**. The disclosure confirms no final consent or evidence that its conditions have been met.

**Push back:**
- Make delivery of an unconditional written Bluefen change-of-control consent, and satisfaction/waiver of all related conditions, a **buyer-benefit condition precedent to Completion**.
- Buyer must be entitled to waive the condition in writing, but Seller should not be able to deem it satisfied merely by delivering a conditional consent.
- If consent is not obtained by long-stop date, Buyer should have termination rights and return of any deposit.
- Obtain a specific warranty that the consent is valid, unconditional and all conditions have been fulfilled or waived.

An obligation to use “reasonable endeavours” does not protect Buyer against loss of a material customer immediately after acquisition.

### 2. Riverlark debt and security must be cleared at or before Completion
**Issue:** The facility has approximately **$3.2m outstanding**, with no discharge of security. Seller proposes a release “following Completion,” contrary to a debt-free/cash-free transaction.

**Push back:**
- Require the Riverlark debt to be repaid **at Completion from the Seller’s proceeds**, under an agreed funds-flow direction.
- Require executed release documents, PPSR releases (where relevant), and a payoff letter confirming the amount required to discharge all liabilities and security.
- Completion should not occur unless releases are delivered in escrow, to take effect immediately on payment.
- Define debt broadly to capture principal, accrued interest, break costs, fees, guarantees, security and any related-party financial indebtedness.

Buyer must not acquire a company carrying debt or security and rely on post-Completion Seller performance.

### 3. Title and fundamental warranties cannot sit within the general cap and survival period
**Issue:** Seller seeks to subject title and capacity warranties to the **20% cap ($4.8m)** and **18-month** limitation.

**Push back:**
- Title, ownership, authority/capacity, power to sell, no encumbrances over shares, and valid issuance of shares should be:
  - **uncapped** (or, at minimum, capped at 100% of purchase price);
  - not subject to de minimis, basket, Buyer-knowledge, disclosure or exclusive-remedy limitations;
  - subject to a materially longer claim period—ordinarily at least the applicable statutory limitation period.
- Add a specific Completion deliverable: original share certificates (if any), signed transfers, board resolutions, register updates and evidence that no options, convertibles, pre-emption rights or encumbrances remain.

DD-012 is only a share-register entry. It is not sufficient assurance of clean, transferable title.

### 4. General warranty limitations are seller-favourable and overextended
**Issue:** The proposed general cap is $4.8m, with a $25,000 de minimis, a $250,000 deductible basket and 18-month survival. Seller also says these limits apply to “all Claims of any nature.”

**Push back:**
- Preserve separate, buyer-protective regimes for:
  - fundamental/title claims;
  - tax claims;
  - fraud, fraudulent concealment, wilful misconduct and deliberate breach;
  - specific indemnities;
  - leakage and purchase-price claims;
  - pre-Completion data/privacy, employment and IP liabilities.
- Narrow the general limitation clause so it applies only to specified **general warranty claims**, not indemnities, tax, covenant breaches, Completion obligations, equitable remedies or statutory claims that cannot lawfully be excluded.
- Seek a higher general cap given the apparent risk profile; at a minimum, do not accept it as a cap on known quantified exposures.
- Make the basket **tipping/first-dollar**, rather than deductible, if possible.
- Exclude related claims arising from the same underlying matter from the de minimis threshold; otherwise a single issue may be artificially fragmented.
- Extend general warranty survival to at least **24 months**. Tax should survive through the relevant assessment/reassessment period plus a buffer.

### 5. Reject general data-room/public-record disclosure and broad Buyer-knowledge exclusions
**Issue:** The Disclosure Letter purports to disclose every matter “contained or referred to” in the entire data room and public registers. Clause 8.3 would also defeat claims for anything known by Buyer or advisers, including matters “discoverable” from the data room or public records.

**Push back:**
- Delete general disclosure of the data room, public registers and matters merely “referred to” in materials.
- Disclosure should qualify warranties only where it is:
  - in the agreed Disclosure Letter;
  - **fairly, specifically and clearly disclosed** against the relevant warranty;
  - sufficiently detailed to identify the nature, scope and reasonably foreseeable consequences of the matter.
- Delete constructive knowledge/discoverability wording. Buyer should not be deemed to know what could have been found by further investigation.
- If a knowledge qualifier is retained at all, limit it to actual knowledge of named senior deal-team members, without imputed adviser knowledge, and exclude Seller fraud, concealment and incomplete/misleading disclosure.
- Preserve warranties despite Buyer due diligence. The Seller is best placed to warrant the Company’s business and records.

The Seller’s own disclosures repeatedly say that critical facts are absent or uncertain. A general disclosure mechanism must not convert incomplete DD into a warranty defence.

### 6. Ironquay IP requires a broader, uncapped specific indemnity and pre-Completion cure
**Issue:** SOW3 Project Materials transfer only on cleared payment of all SOW3 fees; $180,000 remains open, with no proof of payment or assignment. Seller limits the indemnity to the SOW3 payment.

**Push back:**
- Require, before Completion:
  - payment of all outstanding Ironquay amounts;
  - a receipt/release;
  - written confirmation that all relevant IP and Project Materials have vested in the Company, free of security interests and third-party claims;
  - if necessary, a confirmatory assignment with moral-rights consents and further-assurance obligations.
- Obtain a specific indemnity for all loss arising from failure of ownership, use, transferability or infringement risk in respect of Ironquay deliverables—not merely the $180,000 invoice.
- The indemnity should not be subject to general cap, basket, disclosure, knowledge or general time-limit provisions.
- Consider a targeted holdback/escrow until the IP chain of title is confirmed.

The commercial exposure is the value and operability of the developed product/IP, not simply the unpaid invoice.

### 7. Treat DD-006 as a substantive data/privacy risk, not a preliminary operational matter
**Issue:** A data export link may have gone to an unintended external recipient and may contain approximately 1,240 personal-information records. Whether accessed, the full scope, and notification obligations remain unknown.

**Push back:**
- Require Seller to complete and deliver a documented investigation before Completion, including access logs, containment/remediation evidence, affected-data analysis and legal advice/assessment on notification obligations.
- Make satisfactory resolution a Completion condition, or obtain a buyer-benefit termination right if the incident is material or notification/enforcement exposure emerges.
- Include a specific indemnity for all pre-Completion privacy/data-security incident losses, including investigation, forensic, legal, remediation, notification, credit-monitoring, regulatory and third-party costs.
- Require a warranty that there have been no other undisclosed security incidents, notifiable data breaches, regulatory investigations or material non-compliance.
- Ensure the indemnity survives longer than the general warranty period and is outside general limitations.

The disclosure’s uncertainty is precisely why Buyer needs protection; it is not a basis for limiting Seller liability.

### 8. Completion bonuses are a debt-like / transaction-cost item and must not be ignored
**Issue:** DD-005 records **$420,000** of Completion bonuses, but they are excluded from funds flow; payroll tax, superannuation and other costs are unstated.

**Push back:**
- Treat all Completion-triggered bonuses and associated payroll tax, superannuation, leave effects and on-costs as:
  - Seller transaction costs / debt-like items deducted from price; or
  - amounts paid by Seller from its Completion proceeds.
- Define transaction expenses and indebtedness expressly to capture these amounts.
- Require a Completion statement setting out the gross amount, all statutory/on-cost liabilities and payment mechanics.
- Obtain a specific indemnity for any amount not included in the agreed calculation.

These are liabilities created by the sale and should not become Buyer’s post-Completion operating expense.

### 9. Supplier renewals need factual confirmation and a price/indemnity remedy if not ordinary course
**Issue:** Three related renewals total **$330,000**, but Seller does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued, or in the ordinary course.

**Push back:**
- Require copies of all final contracts, renewal dates, notice/termination rights, prepayments, commitments, change-of-control consequences and whether services will be received after Completion.
- Include a pre-Completion covenant preventing new or renewed material commitments other than in the ordinary course and with Buyer consent above an agreed threshold.
- If entered into outside ordinary course, accelerated, non-terminable, or primarily for pre-Completion benefit, require price adjustment or a specific indemnity.
- Ensure working-capital/debt definitions prevent prepayments or accrued supplier costs being double-counted or omitted.

### 10. Tax must have a standalone protection package
**Issue:** Seller says tax is “settled” under the general regime. That is inadequate for historical Company tax liabilities.

**Push back:**
- Include a standalone tax deed/tax covenant covering all pre-Completion tax liabilities, including income tax, GST, PAYG withholding, payroll tax, superannuation-related liabilities, stamp duty, penalties and interest.
- Tax claims should be outside the general cap, basket and 18-month period, subject to an agreed tax-specific cap and survival period aligned with statutory assessment periods.
- Require Seller to control historic-period audits only with Buyer consultation, no settlement affecting Buyer without consent, and prompt reimbursement/indemnification.
- Obtain warranties on tax returns, compliance, disputes, elections, audits, R&D claims (if applicable), payroll obligations and no unpaid tax.

### 11. Strengthen IP warranties beyond the Ironquay issue
**Issue:** Seller seeks to leave IP under the general warranty regime despite an identified chain-of-title concern.

**Push back:**
- Seek robust IP warranties: Company ownership or valid rights to use all material IP; valid contractor/employee assignments; no infringement/misappropriation claims; no open-source licence breach; no undisclosed licences, security interests or restrictions.
- Material IP claims should either have a separate cap/survival period or be protected through a targeted indemnity.
- Require an IP schedule and confirmatory assignments/releases for all material development arrangements.

### 12. Limit exclusive remedy, non-reliance and “all claims” wording
**Issue:** Clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 reportedly make limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to all claims of any nature.

**Push back:**
- Restrict exclusive remedy to contractual warranty claims only, and preserve claims for fraud, misrepresentation to the extent legally permissible, deliberate concealment, specific indemnities, tax covenant claims, debt/leakage, Completion deliverables, injunctive/equitable relief and enforcement costs.
- Non-reliance language should not qualify express warranties, disclosures or Seller-provided information, and must preserve liability for fraudulent or misleading conduct.
- Ensure no clause improperly excludes statutory rights, including rights that cannot be excluded under applicable law.

### 13. Confirm other consent and operational issues
**Office lease / Mossvale:** The disclosures say only notification or assignment restrictions, not share-sale consent requirements. Obtain the full contracts and legal confirmation. If a change-of-control restriction, default or termination right exists, require consent/waiver or targeted indemnity.

**Ordinary course covenant:** From signing to Completion, require operation in the ordinary course; no material contracts, debt, bonuses, unusual payments, disposals, new security, material customer concessions, or data-processing changes without Buyer consent.

## Recommended negotiating position

1. **Do not complete without Bluefen consent and Riverlark payoff/security releases.**
2. **Ring-fence the known risks**—Ironquay IP, DD-006 privacy incident, Completion bonuses and potentially the supplier renewals—with pre-Completion cures, specific indemnities and, where needed, escrow/holdback.
3. **Separate fundamental, tax, indemnity and covenant claims from the general warranty regime.** In particular, reject the proposed application of the 20% cap, thresholds and 18-month limit to all claims.
4. **Delete general data-room/public-record disclosure and constructive Buyer-knowledge language.** Require specific fair disclosure against the relevant warranties.
5. **Rework the funds flow and purchase-price definitions** so Riverlark debt, transaction bonuses and all associated costs are borne by Seller, consistently with the agreed debt-free/cash-free basis.
6. **Obtain proper title, tax and IP protection** rather than relying on a share-register entry and the general warranty package.
